effect_mechanism: Creating or restoring wetland puts aquatic habitat back into a landscape that has very little of it, and the gain shows up at landscape rather than site scale. Catchment-scale wetland creation for simultaneous retention and diversity purposes benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. Each additional created wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness, and the species accumulation curve had not flattened after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity in a landscape where the programme had raised the number of small waters by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. What is planted at the outset persists: the planted basin was still more diverse in plant cover 10 years after planting than the unplanted control, which was more productive but more susceptible to stress [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. On degraded peatland, restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation is said to deliver enhanced biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4].
conditionality: All the measured evidence is temperate and high-income, from created wetlands in a Swedish farming catchment and a pair of created riverine basins in Ohio [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]; the only tropical unit is a statement of potential in a review, bundled with rewetting, with no measurement and no taxon named [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4]. The habitat-density threshold of 30% is a landscape design condition, not an effect size, and the species gain is regional, accumulating across many wetlands rather than appearing at any single site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. effect_mechanism: Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat that the landscape has lost, and the new basins can reach the standard of the old ones. Dual-purpose created wetlands sustained alpha, beta and gamma diversity similar to that of natural lentic water bodies in the region [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2], and the pollution-sensitive stoneflies, mayflies and caddisflies made up almost twice as large a share of richness in the created wetlands, 19%, as in the reference ponds, 10% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. Catchment-scale creation benefited landscape biodiversity, particularly where aquatic habitat density rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each new wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness with no asymptote after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity where small waters had risen by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. Planting at creation left a lasting mark: the planted basin was still more diverse in plant cover 10 years on than the unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7].
conditionality: Most of these findings state a direction without an effect size, which is why the class does not run higher. conditionality: This is a single statement of potential in a review, not a measurement: the wording is that restoration has the potential to deliver these benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4]. The intervention bundles revegetation with rewetting by canal blocking, so no share of any biodiversity gain can be assigned to either component. It applies to Southeast Asian tropical peat and cannot be read across to other wetland types or to farmland biodiversity.

effect_mechanism: Raising the water table switches peat decomposition from aerobic to anaerobic, which is the whole climate case: reinstating the groundwater table reduces aerobic peat decomposition, and anaerobic conditions can substantially decrease carbon dioxide emission [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1]. Restored peatlands have lower carbon emission rates than degraded sites and over time can become net carbon sinks [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1]; carbon dioxide losses fell after Canadian cutaway peat was restored and vegetation re-established, and the carbon balance of Finnish peatlands became a new sink within a few years of restoration [ev_carbon_sequestration_erwi09_1]; a rewetted Irish peatland had a significantly reduced emission factor of 104 g of carbon dioxide carbon per square metre per year, the sign indicating net uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]; and reed canary grass plots on cutover peat had lower global warming potential than bare peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5]. The size of the prize is set by what drained peat is losing, 2 Gt of carbon dioxide a year, nearly a quarter of land-sector emissions and up more than 25% since 1990 [ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]. Outside peat, flooding builds soil carbon: restoring degraded hydric soils has a high potential for sequestrating soil carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2] because flooded wetlands give optimal anoxic conditions for accretion of organic matter [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3], and organic matter in created-wetland surface soils rose by approximately 1% per 3-year period [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], with nitrous oxide fluxes lower when marsh and edge plots were inundated [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9].
conditionality: Rewetting cuts carbon dioxide but raises methane, and the trade-off is in this evidence rather than beside it. The carbon dioxide reduction may be offset by increases in methane emissions from methanogenesis [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2]; at the Irish site the rewetted peatland emitted more methane than natural sites, and the authors concluded that even after a decade of rewetting the global warming potential of rewetted sites was still higher than intact peatlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]. In created wetlands, methane emission in vegetated areas increased significantly once flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, although average emission from pulsed sites stayed below that of permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8]. The only tropical measurements here are nulls or very small. A year after canal damming in Central Kalimantan, carbon dioxide emissions were 7305 then 7444 grams per square metre per year at the forest site and 2781 then 2608 at the deforested burned site, which the authors read as no marked response to the changed hydrology [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2]; the deforested site stayed a weak methane source and the source grew after the dams went in [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3] while the forest floor stayed a weak sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]; and higher water tables had a relatively small effect on the annual methane budgets [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]. The tropical reviews say as much: the outcomes of rewetting studies are inconclusive, and the decomposition reduction may be partly offset by fermentation or anaerobic respiration [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1]; decomposition may continue in the saturated zone with carbon lost through fluvial networks or as methane, and because drainage permanently alters peat structure and chemistry a rewetted peatland cannot be expected to behave like a natural one in its gas exchange [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_2]. The nitrous oxide benefit reaches only as far as the water does, with no difference between flooded and dry periods in upland plots [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10]. Two of the supporting statements are expert assertions of potential with no rate, country or climate zone attached [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3], and the measured gains are temperate, boreal or high-income.

conditionality: Rewetting trades carbon dioxide for methane, and the net result can stay worse than leaving the peat intact. The carbon dioxide saving may be offset by increases in methane from methanogenesis [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2]; the rewetted Irish peatland emitted more methane than natural sites and, even after a decade of rewetting, its global warming potential was still higher than intact peatlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]. Management can reverse the gain outright: the fertilised reed canary grass plot emitted 21,938 kg of carbon dioxide per hectare per year against 8,448 from the natural bog [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_6]. The tropical measurements, the only primary field data here, are nulls. A year of canal damming in Central Kalimantan left carbon dioxide emissions at 7305 then 7444 grams per square metre per year at the forest site and 2781 then 2608 at the deforested burned site, no marked response to the changed hydrology [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2]; the deforested site remained a weak methane source and the source grew after the dams [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3], the forest floor remained a weak sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4], and higher water tables had a relatively small effect on annual methane budgets [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]. The reviews agree the picture is unsettled: rewetting outcomes are inconclusive and the decomposition reduction may be partly offset by fermentation or anaerobic respiration [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1], while a rewetted peatland cannot be expected to behave like a natural peatland in its hydrology, soil ecology or gas exchange, with carbon still leaving through fluvial networks or as methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_2]. Optimally targeted wetland and forest revegetation avoided up to $395,000 of flood damages, 5.3% of total baseline damages [ev_avoided_damage_value_gour20_1]. Conversely, drainage and grazing on China's high-altitude peatlands increased downstream flood risk [ev_flood_hazard_bonn16_4], and wetland protection and restoration are presented as reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2].
